item.title: Cops Bust Botnet of 1.3 Million Android TV Boxes
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
A coalition of security firms working with Japan's National Police Agency has disrupted a botnet of more than 1.3 million Android devices across 200+ countries. "We assess with high confidence that the backdoor and botnet were intentionally developed, deployed, and operated for financial gain by Videostrong Technology," the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said in a blog post. The Register reports: Videostrong Technology is a hardware manufacturer based in Shenzhen, China. It builds Android devices, including home TV boxes and projectors. According to Google, Videostrong deliberately embedded the XCPE backdoor in device firmware and sold access to criminal affiliates, allowing them to install additional malware modules on devices shipped to unsuspecting customers. When buyers connected these devices to their home networks, the preinstalled backdoor allowed operators to create proxy networks and hide malicious traffic using the customers' internet connections without their knowledge.
The firmware's pre-installed management agent purported to be a standard remote-management client, according to TrendAI. It pulled updates from a GitHub page, and connected to a Message Queuing Telemetry Transport (MQTT) server that gave the operator full remote control of each box, allowing them to install and remove apps, change settings, and push updates to the infected devices. Between June 3 and October 1, TrendAI documented more than 3.8 million distinct home and mobile IP addresses connected to the operation.
The coalition also disrupted the command-and-control domains used to manage the affiliate modules. "Because these affiliates each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE, we assess that taking down their C2 domains will sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices," according to GTIG. Google said it had since cut ties with Videostrong, and banned the OEM from making devices with preloaded Google apps.

item.title: Vibe Coded AO3 Clone Site Down After Fanfic Authors Buried It With 2,000 Takedown Notices in a Single Day
item.author: Samantha Cole
item.content:encoded: A vibe-coded site that scraped Archive of Our Own (AO3) fanfiction works, reuploaded them and charged for audiobook versions is down now after the creator said they received over 2,000 takedown requests from authors in the single day it was up., a website that sprung up following last week’s announced weeks-long outage of fanfiction repository AO3, scraped the internet for works to populate the site using “a swarm of AI Agents controlling 40 virtual machines were scraping the internet for all drives, scrapes, and sources,” the site’s creator, named Ganesh, wrote on a page apologizing for the entire project. AO3.life went down on Monday evening following widespread backlash from readers and authors on social media. Before it went down, the ao3.life homepage said, “AO3, saved before it slips away. Search every fandom, ship and trope. Read it here, keep the EPUB, or let it read to you when your eyes get tired.” AO3 went down on Thursday following a security incident, according to the Organization for Transformative Works (OTW) which owns the repository. The site is expected to be down for as long as four weeks. OTW says no data has been lost. Readers and authors are , unable to access the site at all for potentially a month. AO3 hosts nearly 18.5 million works.ao3.life offered works as EPUBs for reading on e-readers, and as AI-generated audiobooks that Ganesh charged for after the first three minutes. They claimed on a page titled “Authors get paid here” that authors would get 91% of the profits, with AO3.life getting 9% to cover “narration and processing” costs. “Your earnings wait for you. You don't need an account here to earn. We hold your share indefinitely until you collect it, however long that takes,” the site said. On AO3, authors can “archive lock” their works, making them visible only to logged-in users, which keeps AI bots like this one from scraping them and also gives better control over how far a work spreads or whether it breaks the containment of the repository’s intended audience. Of course, authors couldn’t access AO3 while it was down to lock their works if they were publicly available before the outage.But some authors reported the archive lock not mattering. “I had everything archive locked on ao3 and it's still all here and I as the author have 0 control over any of my fics on there,” one AO3 author .ao3.life said at the bottom of the homepage that authors could request their works be removed from the site: ”Every work belongs to its author; if one is yours and you want it gone, email legal@ao3.life and it goes.” Proving that you’re the author of the work to ao3.life required authors “leave a note on your AO3 profile so we can confirm it's you,” the site said. But how authors could do that while AO3 was — and still is — completely down is a mystery. A lot of authors clearly used the legal complaints email. “In the time this site has been up, I’ve facilitated over 2,000 takedown requests. It was never my intention to hurt so many authors - and I’m truly sorry to you all. There’s no way to show my sorry [sic] better than taking this site down,” Ganesh wrote. “Why did I charge for AI Slop audiobooks? I doubt anyone knows how expensive it is to run a server like this, especially with the amount of usage this site got. It had 126,592 unique users within 24 hours of going up, and had terabytes of bandwidth in usage. In an attempt to keep the site up, I thought audiobooks were a good option. I sold like 11 audiobooks, if it’s any consolation.”Fanfiction has become a target of AI scraping, repackaging and reselling in recent years. In 2024, I reported on how Etsy sellers turn free fanfiction into printed and bound physical books, then list them for sale for as much as $100 a book. With AO3 down and fans scrambling to find ways to keep consuming the works they miss, some people have started sharing links to Google Drives on Reddit and Discord of works they’d downloaded from the site previously, even if they aren’t the original authors of those works. This has alarmed and angered a lot of writers; whether authors have the right to profit from their works depends on the content and their use of existing intellectual property. Fanfic is typically considered fair use — I can write a Bob and Larry fic without getting sued by Universal Pictures if it’s sufficiently transformative, for example — but selling it could draw the ire of their lawyers, and a potential lawsuit even if I happened to ultimately win it. Authors on AO3 are prohibited by the platform from monetizing their works or linking to payment platforms. “It was never and is not my intention to hurt authors, and I hope every subequent [sic] action I’ve taken is representative of that,” Ganesh said. “From an attempt at revenue sharing, to responding to takedown requests as fast as I could, to taking down the site as a whole.” They signed the note: “Yours truly, a 17 year old from India that thought they were doing something good.”

item.title: China Publicly Discloses Plan For a Lunar Landing Within Three Years
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
At the Seventh Manned Spaceflight Conference in Beijing, Chinese space officials publicly outlined the most detailed roadmap yet for landing astronauts on the Moon "before 2030." Ars Technica reports: China's lunar landings will involve a lunar-orbit rendezvous similar to what NASA did in the 1960s and early 1970s with the Apollo program. However, lacking a rocket as powerful as the Saturn V vehicle, the crew and lunar lander will launch separately to the Moon. According to slides shared on social media, the current plan involves:
- An uncrewed test of the Long March 10A rocket (a single-stick variant, with no boosters) and the Mengzhou spacecraft to low-Earth orbit. Target: early 2027 - An uncrewed test of the larger Long March 10 rocket (a core stage with two boosters) and the Lanyue lunar lander, including descent/ascent from Moon's surface. Target: 2028 - A concurrent launch of two Long March 10 rockets, one carrying uncrewed Mengzhou and the other the Lanyue vehicle; they will dock in lunar orbit. Target: 2029 - Dual launch of Long March 10 rockets, this time with crew on the Mengzhou spacecraft, leading to crewed landing mission. Target: "Before 2030"
The public release of this new information provides a timeline for gauging China's technical progress in its efforts to land humans on the Moon before 2030 and beat NASA and the United States back to the lunar surface. Notably, the plan (for now, at least) omits a mission similar to Apollo 8 or Artemis II, which involved a crew flying out to the Moon and either entering orbit or passing close by before returning to Earth. The Mengzhou vehicle should still get a workout closer to Earth with humans on board as part of missions carrying astronauts to Tiangong, China's space station in low-Earth orbit.

item.title: American Measles Cases Have More Than Doubled Last Year’s Record Totals
item.author: Timothy Geigner
item.content:encoded: As I continue to say, you may be done with the measles, but the measles is not done with you, nor the entire country. Coinciding with the profane installment of RFK Jr. as Secretary of Health and Human Services, 2025 saw the largest number of cases of measles in America in 3 decades. After decades of preaching that established vaccines such as the MMR vaccine were dangerous, caused autism, or were simply not tested enough for safety to be in use, Kennedy oversaw the fruits of his labor as Americans, particularly children, got sicker. Through it all, Kennedy confronted this reality with conspiracy theories, or claiming he had this all under control, or with suggestions that real problem is dirty immigrants infecting Americans.You will note that none of this represents government actually doing anything about the measles outbreaks that are now all over the place in America. Due to this inaction, we eclipsed 2025’s case count all the way back in July. And because of the nature of highly infectious diseases, we have now reached a case count that has more than doubled that of 2025. Something like a quarter of the case counts have come from Pennsylvania alone. Some of the talk from the administration and others is using that fact to try to paint this as a single-state problem, but it absolutely is not. Nor is this an “Amish problem,” which is a claim stemming from the fact that the highest case counts are occurring in counties with large Amish populations, that typically have lower vaccination rates.This is important: that’s just not how infectious diseases work. A problem for one county is a problem for the surrounding counties. A problem for one state is a problem for the country. The American people move and travel freely, and allowing a disease as insidious as measles to fester means it will spread.Vaccination remains the best protection against this disease, even as some breakthrough cases continue to occur among the vaccinated. And it seems that the public is starting to wise up to the fact that Kennedy’s warning against vaccines is bullshit, particularly those closest to the outbreaks.One of the best ways to protect oneself from getting the measles is vaccination, according to health officials. Two doses of measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine known as MMR, is nearly 97% effective against measles, according to the CDC. One dose is about 93% effective.In Pennsylvania, the health department said healthcare providers have seen more residents interested in getting vaccinated for measles. Across the state, more than 39,000 measles vaccines were administered during the first three weeks of October – higher than an average of 25,000 vaccines administered across the state in one month, the health department said.Getting to the other side of all of this will not be done quickly. It’s going to take time. Vaccination rates in America continue to fall overall, which is going to be a headwind against getting measles in America under control. Perhaps changes will be made after the midterms that will lead to actual government action on this problem. Still, it will take time.Sadly, a good first goal here would be for there to be fewer measles cases in 2027 than what will be a record-breaking total in 2026. Given that measles was declared eliminated in 2000, a goal like that is embarrassing. But at least it would be a start.But for that, we need federal leadership that just isn’t in place at the moment.

item.title: New Studies Confirm Today’s Academic Publishing System Is A Terrible Deal For Society
item.author: Glyn Moody
item.content:encoded: Walled Culture has just written about the possibility that recent AI breakthroughs might accelerate a move to open access, at least in the field of mathematics. It would be particularly welcome against a backdrop of relatively slow progress in the open access world. That is not because the need for different business models that provide free access for all to published research is less, but simply because the obstacles and difficulties faced by researchers remain largely unknown to the wider public, and therefore removing them is not a priority. To the outsider, the world of academic publishing seems to be flourishing; and it is, for publishers, but it remains a source of friction and frustration for the people actually writing the papers that are published. The wider dynamics within the world of academic publishing remain opaque, particularly concerning the costs and benefits. Two new independent studies from the University of Sydney Business School may help to change that. The first, entitled “The Cost Of Knowledge” notes a remarkable omission in the discussions about academic publishing and the move to open access:Debates about the economics of scholarly publishing typically focus on subscription prices, article processing charges, publisher revenues, and profit margins. Much less attention is paid to the costs incurred in producing the research that makes scholarly publishing possible.Publishers love to talk about how much it costs to produce academic journals, and why the charges for publishing have to be so high, but they gloss over the fact that publication is merely the end stage in the much longer and more complex process of conducting and reporting research. The new University of Sydney Business School research seeks to estimate how much that work before publication typically costs, in order to provide context for the publication fees. The researchers identified eight key stages of article production where costs could be estimated:ideation and conception; grant seeking and approval, where applicable; ethics approval; performance of the study and data analysis; writing and manuscript preparation, up to first submission; peer and conferencing feedback; journal editorial work; and peer review and revision cycles. Rather than costing these stages as discrete, sequential blocks, we represent them within a single integrated estimation record that recognises the overlaps between them, the resources they share, principally researcher time, but also institutional infrastructure and administrative support, and the cumulative effect of revising as a manuscript moves iteratively between stages.The final result of applying that methodology is striking:Drawing on the ingredients method, this paper attempts to construct a fuller account of that process, tracing the resources and associated costs consumed from ideation through to acceptance. While our estimate of approximately US$70,000 is necessarily conservative and open to refinement, it points to a substantial investment of labour, infrastructure, governance arrangements, and public resources that are essential [for] the production of a published article long before publication itself becomes possible.To place that figure in context:Grossman and Brembs (2021) put the cost of [the service provide by academic publishers] at around US$400 per article. Set against our estimate of approximately US$70,000 to produce a social science article, the publishing function appears to represent less than 1% of the total resources invested in creating the research. Even using Grossman and Brembs’ upper estimate of approximately US$1,000 per article, publication costs account for only around 1.4% of total production costs. This comparison highlights a central tension in contemporary scholarly communication given that after substantial public and institutional investment in producing research, access to the resulting knowledge is frequently restricted through subscription-based publishing models.The implications of that relatively small figure are important:Viewed in this way, the estimate draws attention to a structural asymmetry within contemporary scholarly communication where the production of knowledge depends heavily upon publicly funded institutions, publicly supported research, and academic labour, and this provides a largely unaccounted for subsidy to private sector publishers, underwriting at least some of the financial returns they enjoyThat is, with every paper that appears in their titles, academic publishers are generating significant profits not only thanks to free academic labor in the form of peer review, but also thanks to long-term and massive levels of public funding. Their ability to free ride on such invisible subsidies is never acknowledged by publishers, which like to claim all the credit for making papers available, as if they were benefactors underpinning the entire system of research. In fact, by imposing high and unjustified publication costs on academic institutions and their funders, publishers act as a serious obstacle to the dissemination of publicly-funded research, denying people their right to access the academic work they pay for.The results of that “structural asymmetry” are explored in the second piece of research from the University of Sydney Business School, with the self-explanatory title “How Profitable are the Big Four Publishers” – the “Big Four” being RELX (Elsevier), Informa (Taylor & Francis), Springer Nature and Wiley:The evidence shows that academic publishing has been an exceptionally resilient and profitable business. Despite periods of major economic disruption, including the global financial crisis (2008) and the Covid-19 pandemic (2020-2022), all four publishers remained profitable throughout the period examined. For the diversified firms, academic publishing consistently generated the highest profit margins within their business portfolios.Taken together, the findings suggest that the Big Four are not only securing significant financial returns from scholarly communication but are also extending their influence across the wider research ecosystem. The report raises questions about the distribution of economic value, control of research infrastructure and the governance of publicly funded knowledge.The two new reports are unlikely to change the state of open access quickly or dramatically. But their value lies in the fact that they confirm – with data – that the current academic publishing system is a terrible deal not just for researchers and institutions, but also for the governments and public which fund it.

item.title: Study Claims Vizio Simply Ignores 'Smart' TV Spying Opt Out Requests
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Techdirt: Recently, reports emerged that LG TVs are sniffing around your local network, and even listening to your local environment, even when the TV is purportedly "off." Some of those voice commands were then stored in plain text and uploaded to the internet. LG's response? To deny everything. [...] That latter point is central to a new study out of Northeastern that conducted 5,943 experiments across twelve commercial "smart" TV devices. The researchers found that most smart TVs utilize automatic content recognition (ACR), a technology that captures audio or video snapshots of viewed content and then monetizes that data to help build personalized profiles of viewers.
TV makers insist that users are supposed to be able to opt out, but the choice simply doesn't work across a large segment of TVs. Companies like Vizio simply ignored the consumer requests entirely more often than not: "We find that the advertised ACR opt-out fully suppresses ACR-attributable traffic on only four operating systems; on Samsung Tizen traffic consistent with ACR activity persists in more than 60% of evaluated scenarios, and on Vizio SmartCast a content correlated endpoint hosted on Amazon Kinesis continues to receive traffic in 100% of opted-out scenarios."
[...] The researchers say since they can't see the precise scope of what's being collected due to encryption, they're unsure whether Vizio is technically violating its FTC agreement (not that we have a current FTC that would care if they were): "The opt-out setting has no observable effect on traffic sent to this endpoint; however, we cannot inspect the payload due to encryption so we cannot confirm whether this violates the FTC settlement." Results of whether opting out of ACR tracking actually stopped ACR tracking were all over the map. Roku, for example, ignores opt-out requests when users are watching Roku's own channels. None of the smart TV vendors track Netflix viewing for fear of violating agreements with the streaming giant. Samsung's opt out function was more likely to actually work when a user was watching antenna broadcasts.
On two Smart TV platforms, personal viewing data collected by ACR remains unencrypted, despite years of bad press and scandal on the subject. Many appear to be violating the law, but because U.S. regulatory oversight has been gutted, they see no meaningful accountability. That includes smart TV OS' like VIDAA, which is most prominently found on Hisense and Toshiba smart TVs: "VIDAA OS sends ACR data to servers run by Unruly over MQTT without encryption, so anyone on the network path between the TV and those servers can read it. Each message carries a Client ID, a permanent identifier for the TV that can't be reset, along with the time zone, the app name, the input (antenna, HDMI), the antenna channel and an audio fingerprint."

Collective licensing and machine-readable consent tools are in use, and that should drive the factor four analysis.No explicit ask; the argument favors plaintiffs.Copyright law professors (incl. Julia Powles, Trevor Reed, Marketa Trimble, Bhamati Viswanathan; full list in the brief's appendix)Training and RAG copying is direct infringement. In these works expression is inseparable from facts and ideas, and copyright has never allowed wholesale copying of expression to reach the underlying knowledge.Progressive Democrats of America, RadicalxChange, Tech Oversight Project, Young People's Alliance, Prof. Walter Scheirer (lead author David Atkinson)Defendants want “GenAI exceptionalism.” If their use is fair, almost any human's unlicensed use would be too. Public availability doesn't create an implied license.Economic argument: unlicensed AI use erodes incentives and degrades the information ecosystem, and the split of value is grossly inequitable. Licenses should divide the gains.Attaches an economics paper (51 pp.).Loss of local news makes government costlier and less accountable, communities less safe and democracy weaker. Claimed public benefits can't outweigh that.Focuses on RAG: the copying is the violation and the output shows a substitutive purpose. Harm to news is ongoing, and spreading the copying across sessions doesn't excuse it.AAN Publishers, Inst. for Rural Journalism, LION Publishers, Nat'l Ass'n of Hispanic Publications, Rebuild Local News Coalition, Solutions Journalism Network, NewsGuild-CWA, SPJStrong copyright gives small outlets leverage for compensation. Today only big outlets get AI deals, so a ruling for the NYT would push AI companies toward licensing that pays local news.AI startups: BandLab, Boomy, Created by Humans, Credtent, Splice, Newstex, ProRata.ai, SourceAudio, Cashmere (Vandal AI), Voice-SwapLicensed training hasn't priced developers out. Licensing creates markets, pays creators and reduces legal risk, so requiring permission won't slow innovation.Defendants haven't shown that machine-scale training is equivalent to human creative reuse, which is the premise of transformativeness. Rebalancing the IP Clause is for Congress.The motion says it supports plaintiffs, but the brief “urges no outcome.”William Morris Endeavor (WME)Factor four: AI companies already license copyrighted works, voices and likenesses, and WME negotiates those deals. Unauthorized training and AI replicas harm that market, and lost licensing fees count as market harm.Supports the news plaintiffs. Filed only in the NYT case (23-cv-11195).

item.title: Governments Worldwide Are Shaping What AI Can Say About Politics
item.author: Jordi Calvet-Bademunt
item.content:encoded: With the U.S. midterms this week, about 1 in 5 voters has asked AI chatbots about elections and politics, a recent survey found.But many voters may not know that governments around the world increasingly shape what chatbots can say. And because many tech companies apply the same policies worldwide, the answers American voters get may be shaped by governments at home and abroad.Censorship masked as safetyIt’s important that governments tackle these harms. But, in our assessment, some governments use legitimate concerns like these as a pretext to control political discussion, particularly chatbot responses about those in power.Vietnam shows what such content controls can mean for dissidents, including those in exile. A Vietnamese court sentenced two activists, who live in Germany, to 17 years each in prison in December 2025 for spreading anti-state material. Prosecutors accused them of using AI to fake voices and images of Vietnamese leaders, illustrating how prosecutions can target political criticism.Foreign rules, domestic impactSome of these government measures only affect people residing in their countries. Other statutes cross borders.European rules also affect what chatbots say about politics.And the Dutch Data Protection Authority tested four chatbots before the 2025 national election and found that the political middle ground “virtually disappears” in their voting advice. It urged providers to “prevent their systems from being used for voting advice.”These rules can be used to pressure platforms.In 2024, Thierry Breton, then the EU’s top digital rules enforcer, reminded Elon Musk of his legal obligations before Musk’s live interview with then-presidential candidate Donald Trump on X, warning against the spread of “harmful content.”The United States is no exceptionThreats to Americans’ access to information do not come only from abroad.In 2025, President Trump issued an executive order on “Preventing Woke AI in the Federal Government.” It requires the AI models the government buys to be “truth-seeking,” ideologically neutral and not favoring ideas such as “diversity, equity and inclusion.”“Truth-seeking” may sound like an objective, neutral term, but it can mean very different things to different people. Take media reporting: The president recently banned three news outlets from the White House for reporting “FICTION and LIES” and dismissed media polls as “fake.”More recently, the Federal Trade Commission has suggested that AI companies that steer answers toward undisclosed ideological or biased objectives might break consumer protection law.A 2025 Pew Research Center survey found that 8 in 10 Americans believe Republican and Democratic voters cannot agree on basic facts. In other words, as our report notes, government mandates to seek truth are often driven by ideological belief systems, particularly on political issues.What does this mean for voters? When you ask your chatbot about the elections, treat the answer as a starting point. Keep in mind that governments, both foreign and domestic, may try to influence the answer. AI responses should not replace your critical thinking at the ballot box.Jordi Calvet-Bademunt is a Research Fellow and Visiting Scholar of Political Science at Vanderbilt University and The Future of Free Speech think tank.

item.title: The New York Times Sues Brave Web Browser For AI Scraping, Bypassing Paywalls
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
The New York Times and several other publishers have sued (PDF) Brave Software, accusing the browser maker of scraping their websites without permission and helping users bypass paywalls. The Verge reports: According to a complaint (PDF) filed by the companies that run New York Daily News, the Chicago Tribune, and the Orlando Sentinel, Brave Software has monetized its index of scraped websites by, in part, providing AI companies with paid access to "real-time online content from the Brave Index." The AI companies then use that index to train their models, access content to "respond to specific user queries," or both. Brave has allegedly provided "stolen copyrighted content" to "many" AI companies including Anthropic, Perplexity, Mistral, xAI, and Cohere. Brave also promotes "hundreds of top publishers" as being accessible through its "Paywall blocker" feature in its browser.
"Brave has never asked for the Publishers' permission to access their websites, much less to copy the material and provide it to users or other AI companies," the complaint says. "On the contrary, as noted above, Brave allows its users to bypass the Publishers' paywalls without their consent, and has taken other steps that prevent the Publishers from blocking Brave's access to the Publishers' websites. Brave has never compensated the Publishers for the unlawful use, copying, and distribution of the Publishers' copyrighted content." "While we believe in the ethical and responsible use and development of AI, Brave has flouted established copyright law and ignored repeated requests by The Times to stop its infringing conduct," Graham James, an NYT spokesperson, says in a statement. "We filed this lawsuit to hold Brave accountable for stealing our content to power its own products and to provide it to some of the most prominent and well resourced generative AI companies in the world."

item.title: Microsoft's Canada Timezone Troubles Leave Admins Fixing Calendars, Pretending They're In Bogota
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
Microsoft is scrambling to fix time-zone problems across Outlook, Power Automate, Fabric, SharePoint and other products after parts of Canada stopped observing seasonal clock changes on November 1. "The company has confirmed problems across a chunk of its software estate, leaving some customers facing incorrect times, broken schedules and a collection of workarounds while Redmond catches up," reports The Register. From the report: Outlook users have been left with the most homework. Switching to the new Canadian time zones won't automatically update existing calendar entries, meaning that meetings scheduled after November 1 are potentially an hour out of whack. Microsoft advises users to change their Outlook calendar time zone, then update upcoming events and meetings to use it. For meetings involving other people, only the organizer can make the change.
Recurring meetings come with an additional treat: changing the time zone resets any previously moved occurrences, which then have to be recreated. Anyone with a calendar full of recurring meetings may wish to put the kettle on first. Microsoft is working on an Exchange Online PowerShell cmdlet to remediate non-recurring meetings, but according to its guidance, that's not due until later this week. A fix for recurring meetings remains "in development," with an ETA yet to be confirmed.
Things get stranger with Power Automate and Fabric, where Microsoft's temporary fix involves pretending you're somewhere else entirely. Depending on the product and province, that could mean Saskatchewan, Arizona or, for Manitobans, Bogota. Because apparently time zones weren't confusing enough already. SharePoint On-Prem customers, meanwhile, have to wait until November 10 for the correct time zones to arrive, while Power Pages users could see server-formatted dates appear an hour out until a service fix lands. Microsoft's current milestone for that is December 12.

item.title: Sam Altman’s Case Against Your RAM Is Efficient. That’s The Problem
item.author: Mike Masnick
item.content:encoded: By now it’s likely you’ve heard of the whole concept of the AI paperclip maximizer problem — a hypothetical first put forth by Nick Bostrom — suggesting that a misaligned AI system that looks to optimize on the wrong single thing (in this case creating paperclips) could lead to the end of humanity. Specifically, the thought experiment is that if you have a sufficiently powerful AI tool that is told to “maximize” the creation of paperclips, it might decide the best way to do that is to seize control of all resources and dedicate them solely to making paperclips. And, naturally, that might include grinding up humans, either as raw material for paperclips or as fuel to power the paperclip factory.The supposed “lesson” of this is to be cautious about these AI tools, though I think the actual lessons are twofold: (1) thought experiments can only take you so far and (2) never over optimize on a single metric. Indeed, this was part of what our recent series, The Metric is Not the Mission, was all about.Anyway, everyone in the AI world knows about the whole paperclip thing. I guarantee you Sam Altman knows about it. He has praised the book where Bostrom put forth the hypothetical, claiming that it was “the best thing I’ve seen” on the topic of “will AI kill us all.” And he’s joked about it in a memey way:But it’s not clear that he truly has internalized that lesson regarding not optimizing on just a single thing. Last week he went on John Collison’s (co-founder of Stripe) “Cheeky Pint” podcast to talk about the state of AI.A bunch of the headlines focused on one specific thing that he said, however, that it’s “quite terrible” for people to be wasting RAM in home machines over having them working full steam in a data center somewhere. The context here matters a bit. Collison catches Altman a bit off guard by asking “how’s the compute shortage going?” just as Altman takes a big gulp from his pint of beer, and you see Altman try not to laugh/spit out his beer, before there’s an obvious cut in the video, where he recomposes himself.They then have a discussion about the increasing demand for compute, Altman talks about how they’re working on having robots build “self-replicating data centers” (what?!?) to which Collison rightly interjects that the problem with data centers right now isn’t the lack of labor available to build them. Collison then shifts the conversation back to the stuff that most people care about: the fact that RAM prices have increased dramatically recently, which is jacking up the price of everything from computers to phones.Collison notes that people keep saying the market should take care of this: if prices keep going up, shouldn’t Adam Smith’s “invisible hand” motivate more companies to make more RAM and ease the shortage? Altman shows that he’s not a big believer in the invisible hand of the market concept:: My observation, the compute stuff is they say: “The solution to high prices is high prices.” And it’s like, okay.Step 1: We have the high prices for memory, and GPUs, and everything. The solutions should be here any moment now. How are we doing on the solutions front?: And I’m not saying this is OpenAI’s job. I feel this is the invisible hand’s job, right? Memory’s gotten really expensive. So, new memory makers are going to flood the market any moment now.: I think the invisible hand is failing right now. I mean, the invisible hand… It has like a checkered track record at best. But, I think it’s not quite working here.He then points out that, for decades, DRAM was a commodity product with razor-thin margins and barely any profits. His argument is that memory makers aren’t willing to expand much because they’re afraid that the bubble might burst and they’d have overbuilt (which… might not be wrong?).Of course, Altman leaves out of this the fact that OpenAI has basically tried to corner the market on RAM, trying to lock up 40% of the world’s supply without even guaranteeing that it will follow through on the actual purchase orders. I mean, I think that alone would have at least impact on the current price for RAM, wouldn’t it?Collison pushes a bit further, and still wants to know why others aren’t getting into the memory market, and even (half jokingly?) suggests Intel could get into the market — a reference to one of the key parts of Intel’s lore and mystique: the Andy Grove decision in 1985 to get completely out of the memory chip business to focus on processors, which got a bunch of recent attention when Intel’s current CEO suggested the (struggling) company might reverse that decision 40 years later.That brings Altman around to the critical quote regarding local RAM, in which he dismisses the argument that local inference is important, as a way of suggesting that the more efficient use of memory would be in large datacenters where it can be utilized at a much higher rate:Oh, I think there are all of these ways where the supply chain—it’s just super non-obvious.An example of this is people…A lot of people want local inference. And somehow, they assume that the problem is solved now. Because, we are going to have open-source models. We’re going to be able to run them on our computers. And so we’re not going to need all the stuff in the data center.But from a global allocation perspective, actually,it’s quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the world’s limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer. And, being used—Mm-hmm. 5% of the time. You want maximum utilization in the cloud if you’re trying to deal with this very supply constrained environment.And somehow everyone’s… many people’s intuition is the opposite of that.So he’s correct… in one very, very, very narrow sense of this quote. If you are interested in dealing with the current “world’s limited supply of DRAM” he’s not wrong that it is more “efficient” to have that RAM be in a data center and then rented out to you. And he’s not exactly wrong that if everyone just paid per token for remote compute, the cost of RAM in your own PC would matter a lot less.But… he’s kinda missing the larger point: that people are not just focused on optimizing for the most efficient use of memory. They’re not just optimizing for what’s best for “the global supply chain of RAM makers.” They have other concerns — and other uses beyond AI — as well, such as their own sovereignty and control over their own tools and systems. There’s a reason my essay on the need for decentralization (including in AI) went so viral a few months back.And it’s not because people think they’re single-handedly going to solve the global supply crisis in DRAM by running everything locally. It’s because we’ve seen what happens when a central provider controls key parts of our stack, and the results are very, very, very bad.Using open weight models on local hardware may not be the most efficient for the exact price of RAM (which, again, Altman tried to corner the market on), but it certainly leads to much more actual user empowerment by people who want to use these tools, but without outsourcing control to someone like Altman.In a pure “efficiency” model where you are solely optimizing on what’s the most cost efficient way to use memory the answer would be to have it in datacenters where you’d benefit from both economies of scale as well as flexible utilization. But that has consequences. It’s the same logic by which a fascist dictator may seem “more efficient” to those sick of democratic quirks and bureaucratic red tape. It only sounds good if your mental model is completely screwed up and simplistic.In both cases, you’re talking about a very simplified mental model, optimizing on a suboptimal point. Personal autonomy over our tools and our systems is more important than making your data center more efficient, Sam. The paperclip problem comes from focusing on a narrow metric and over optimizing on it. And in this clip, Sam is paperclipping RAM.

item.title: Marvell to Buy Lumentum In $115 Billion Bet On AI Connectivity
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded: Marvell has agreed to acquire optical components maker Lumentum in an all-stock deal with an implied enterprise value of $115 billion. "AI infrastructure is undergoing a fundamental architectural shift toward optical connectivity, creating an opportunity that comes along once in a generation," said Marvell Chairman and CEO Matt Murphy. "The companies that move first and help define this transition will set the standard for decades to come." CNBC reports: Through the acquisition, Marvell said it can combine electrical and optical technologies to meet accelerating and shifting AI connectivity demands across regions and systems. Lumentum shareholders will receive 4.5 Marvell shares for each Lumentum share under the agreement. The deal is expected to close during the first half of 2028. Marvell's takeover marks one of the most significant bets on AI in 2026 and comes despite recent concerns over the long-term sustainability of infrastructure spending.

item.title: Voting in 2026 Is Getting an AI Slop 'I Voted' Sticker
item.author: Matthew Gault
item.content:encoded: It’s a small pleasure, but receiving an “I Voted” sticker after casting my ballot is one of my favorite parts of the whole voting process. I slap the sticker on my chest and spend the rest of the day feeling like I accomplished a little something. I participated in democracy and everyone who sees me will know it. Artificial intelligence robbed me of that small joy this year and replaced it with a small horror. My “I Voted” sticker is AI-generated slop. Getting a little sticker when you vote has been a tradition in the US . It’s a symbol of the election cycle. People take selfies and post them or share them with friends. It’s a celebration of democracy and a small way to pressure people into going to the ballot box. The voting sticker has been subject to every kind of discourse imaginable. Are “I Voted” stickers worth the cost? Wondered Marketplace in 2020. A cemetery in New York has spent time and money of Susan B Anthony because voters coat it in stickers during voting season. In 2008, companies like Starbucks and Ben and Jerry’s of election laws for offering free treats to people who showed their “I Voted” stickers.It’s appropriate but depressing that I got an AI slop “I Voted” sticker in 2026, the year it feels like the mainstream began to reckon with AI.My sticker is ugly. It’s a busy circular nightmare. “I Voted” is spelled out in small bronze text at the top of the ring. Bronze laurels encircle a bronze bald eagle that stretches atop the American flag. Below this is more text: “250 YEARS ANNIVERSARY” and "SEMIQUENCENTENNIAL.” Below that, another line reads — as best I can tell — “CEKEVPATIVG EDELDOA.” I assume this was meant to say “CELEBRATING FREEDOM," but whoever churned out this slop wasn’t using the latest models and the fine detail is lost.I put the sticker on reluctantly, but I was not proud. I sent a photo of the offending sticker to journalist friends with my face cropped out. They immediately noticed it was AI-generated. I did not post my sticker online. I shared it with no one else. My democratic joy turned to shame.A few hours later, a friend sent me a selfie. He’d just left the voting booth. His sticker was beautiful, tasteful, a testament to the subtle art of the “I Voted” sticker. A red ring enclosed a blue field. The crescent and palmetto (symbols of South Carolina) sat elegantly behind a bold white “I VOTED.”His sticker catches the eye. Passers-by will know exactly what the sticker says. They know he voted. Anyone looking at my sticker will wonder how I spilled some bronze paint on my chest. I trembled with indignation. One town over from me they’re giving out the good stickers and I’m stuck with slop. First my town of 12,000 installs 33 Flock cameras and now this? I spent some time scrolling through social media to see other “I Voted” stickers. So many are so beautiful. Michigan runs a contest where students can submit their own idea for a sticker and the state will print up the winners. , , and several other places around the country do the same. Louisiana commissions local artists to produce . My mouth hung up in a jealous scowl as I stared at pictures of New Orleanians bedecked with a sticker showing a hand drawn trumpet blasting out “I Voted” alongside Mardi Gras beads.Only Denton, Texas (another place I’ve lived, weirdly) seems to also have AI-generated slop stickers. Denton’s sticker is, at least, personalized. The city’s court house is in the corner looking more or less correct. The “I Voted” is large and centered in the sticker itself. Like mine, the image is too busy. Too much text, too many fireworks, and the inclusion of the Liberty Bell clutters the whole thing up. The central message — “I Voted” — is bright white. It doesn’t sink into a busy bronze soup like on my sticker.Complaining about AI-slop “I Voted” stickers may seem trivial in a world where AIs are choosing targets in warzones and vibecoders are every piece of software ever written. But these little things are important. These small annoyances pile up until things like are so ubiquitous that you don’t notice them anymore. The AI drive-thru and one day you stop worrying about it so much. You get an ugly AI slop “I Voted” sticker and you slap it on or toss it out. Enough of these build up until you don’t notice that AI all around you. And then, one day, it’s all normal.Right now we’re figuring out where our AI lines are. Society is negotiating what the future will look like. We’re , figuring out to keep our bosses happy, and learning what we will and won’t abide.Me? I draw the line at AI-generated “I Voted” stickers.

item.title: Reaping and sowing, CEO edition
item.author: Samantha Cole
item.content:encoded: It’s rare to see an executive go from fucking around to finding out so quickly. That’s what happened last week when Proton CEO Andy Yen announced he was canceling a planned re-interview process for almost all current employees that would have checked if they’re using AI enough. This follows extreme backlash from Proton users and workers against the company's aggressive pivot to AI. It’s been a wild ride internally, several employees past and present have shared with 404 Media.On Friday, Andy Yen, the CEO of Proton, cancelled a series of nearly company-wide ‘re-interviews’ that would have forced employees to explain how they are using AI, with the clear intention that they may be fired if not using it enough in the eyes of Proton leadership, according to six current Proton employees and audio of an around two hour all-hands meeting obtained by 404 Media.The move came after 404 Media published an investigation on Thursday, which showed how Yen was aggressively pushing AI across Proton, in some cases despite security concerns from employees. In one exchange, an employee in the company’s security Slack channel urged Proton to at least take a few days to pentest newly written code before pushing it live. “That’s bullshit and loser thinking. Of course it’s possible to be fast and secure,” Yen wrote in the channel at the end of August. “Stop thinking always of how to be slower, and focus more on how to be faster.” Yen added, “stop lovingly handcrafting all our code and use AI more.”The re-interview cancellations likely don’t address the concerns of many Proton users, who are more focused on Proton’s deprioritization of security; many Proton users have blasted the company’s leadership on social media over the last 24 hours and explicitly called for Yen to resign.Kinktober has come and gone. But Archive of Our Own (AO3), a massive repository for fanfiction and creative writing, is still down, and might be down for as long as a month after going down for "maintenance" following a security incident last week. The Organization for Transformative Works (OTW), the non-profit organization that runs AO3, posted on its status page that the site restoration will take around two weeks, but could take up to a month.People are coping how they can.And they’re turning to anything but Wattpad to fill the void. item.title: Study Claims Vizio Simply Ignores ‘Smart’ TV Spying Opt Out Requests
item.author: Karl Bode
item.content:encoded: For decades now we’ve documented how while “smart” TV makers are obsessed with making money off of in-home surveillance (which is now more profitable than the actual TV), they do an abysmal job protecting the data they collect. They also routinely don’t respect consumer choice when users say they don’t want to participate in the full scope of hyper-commercialized mass surveillance.That latter point is central to a new study out of Northeastern that conducted 5,943 experiments across twelve commercial “smart” TV devices. The researchers found that most smart TVs utilize automatic content recognition (ACR), a technology that captures audio or video snapshots of viewed content and then monetizes that data to help build personalized profiles of viewers.TV makers insist that users are supposed to be able to opt out, but the choice simply doesn’t work across a large segment of TVs. Companies like Vizio simply ignored the consumer requests entirely more often than not:“We find that the advertised ACR opt-out fully suppresses ACR-attributable traffic on only four operating systems; on Samsung Tizen traffic consistent with ACR activity persists in morethan 60% of evaluated scenarios, and on Vizio SmartCast a content correlated endpoint hosted on Amazon Kinesis continues to receive traffic in 100% of opted-out scenarios.”These companies have been awful for a long while now, and U.S. regulation of the sector has varied between soggy and inconsistent. Many smart TV manufacturers fail to encrypt sensitive data, or remove features if you refuse to have your daily viewing habits measured and monetized (by say, disconnecting your TV from the internet). Vizio was fined $2.2 million by the FTC back in 2017 for failing to tell customers that their televisions were spying on them. The company also wound up facing a $17 million lawsuit that wound up giving consumers somewhere between $13 and $31 (lawyers in the case saw $5.6 million in fees). The researchers say since they can’t see the precise scope of what’s being collected due to encryption, they’re unsure whether Vizio is technically violating its FTC agreement (not that we have a current FTC that would care if they were):“The opt-out setting has no observable effect on traffic sent to this endpoint; however, we cannot inspect the payload due to encryption so we cannot confirm whether this violates the FTC settlement.”Results of whether opting out of ACR tracking actually stopped ACR tracking were all over the map. Roku, for example, ignores opt-out requests when users are watching Roku’s own channels. None of the smart TV vendors track Netflix viewing for fear of violating agreements with the streaming giant. Samsung’s opt out function was more likely to actually work when a user was watching antenna broadcasts. On two Smart TV platforms, personal viewing data collected by ACR , despite years of bad press and scandal on the subject. Many appear to be violating the law, but because U.S. regulatory oversight has been gutted, they see no meaningful accountability. That includes smart TV OS’ like VIDAA, which is most prominently found on Hisense and Toshiba smart TVs:“VIDAA OS sends ACR data to servers run by Unruly over MQTT without encryption, so anyone on the network path between the TV and those servers can read it. Each message carries a Client ID, a permanent identifier for the TV that can’t be reset, along with the time zone, the app name, the input (antenna, HDMI), the antenna channel and an audio fingerprint.The app name alone can be revealing. We saw ACR on apps such as VIDAA Kids, which raises concerns under the U.S. children’s privacy law (COPPA), and Christianity and Money. VIDAA’s own HOME OS app sent show and film titles in place of the app name.”Keep in mind these researchers just focused on ACR — or video, image, or audio snippets taken to track your viewing and build a profile on you. There are numerous other ways smart TVs can track you — and numerous other avenues via which your traffic is being surveilled by everybody along the chain, including your telecom provider. This persists because companies do not fear U.S. regulators, because U.S. regulators have been largely lobotomized via corruption. The United States also remains too corrupt to base even a baseline privacy law for the internet era or regulate the data brokers that further monetize much of this data. Still the researchers were nice enough to provide regulators a path, should they someday choose to do their jobs.

item.title: Itch Is Being Flooded By AI-Generated Garbage
item.author: EditorDavid
item.content:encoded:
The number of game pages being created per-day on Itch has doubled, the indie games site announced Saturday on Bluesky. When asked why, they responded: "take a guess."
As the gaming news site Aftermath puts it, "the surge has been almost entirely down to AI-created garbage racing onto the platform as the popularity of vibe-coded theft, copycats and machine-built slop explodes."
Back in 2024, when the spectre of AI-'created' video games was still in its infancy, indie platform itch.io decided that the best it could do to combat this growing threat was, like Valve has done with Steam, institute a voluntary 'AI' filter when adding new projects to the site. By November 2026, as itch buckles under the weight of new AI-generated 'games' pouring onto the site, that filter is proving about as robust as a wet paper bag.... Shopfronts are being deluged by this shit, and it's making it a terrible user experience for customers.
And while in Valve's case there's a compelling case for stronger human moderation of the store, I'm not sure that's a viable option for a relatively tiny, community-run platform like itch... [A]t time of writing I visited the latest releases section and there was still a huge number of clearly AI-generated titles (or titles making extensive use of AI in their visual assets) which made no use of itch's voluntary tag system.
The issue here isn't that these games are making money--itch themselves say in a reply that while the number of projects listed has doubled, "the number of downloads and purchases has not"--it's that an inability to combat this surge makes the site worse for every single person using it. It gets harder to find real games, for example, and it also makes the shopfront look like a clearance rack.

item.title: Bad Flock Info Leads Police To Tow Wrong Car, Then Towing Company Totals It
item.author: EditorDavid
item.content:encoded:
"Police continue to blindly trust Flock cameras above and beyond the evidence in front of their own eyes," reports Jalopnik.com.
"After incorrectly connecting Rosalyn Crump's car to a shooting that had occurred the previous day, police had her car towed and impounded as evidence, reports Moneywise..."
According to WWBT 12 On Your Side, Richmond, Virginia, police didn't have a license plate number for the suspect's car, making it impossible to search Flock's records for that plate. Flock cameras collect more than just license plate information, so police searched for a make, model, color, and approximate model year. Based on this extremely vague description, police zeroed in on Crump's 2012 Hyundai Elantra. Around 2 a.m. they started looking through the windows with flashlights to see what was in plain sight, which isn't technically a "search" — at least, not one that would require a warrant... [Crump was asleep, but left her home to speak to the police officers to tell them they had the wrong car. But they didn't believe her.]
Other body cam footage shows an officer expressing doubt that Crump's car is the right one, since child seats and other items inside seem inconsistent with a shooting. Another officer replies, "Don't be surprised if they would have set that up like that." Instead of believing the evidence, or Crump, or interviewing witnesses who could have corroborated her story, police called Seibert's Towing to impound the car...
[Later] Police identified a similar-looking car that seemed to be actually connected to the shooting, and released Crump's Elantra. Nobody actually told Crump this until four days later. Seibert's told Moneywise that police didn't actually release the car until then. Either way, they didn't tell her that Seibert's had ripped the front bumper off during the towing process — leaving the car undrivable — until she arrived to pick it up. Seibert's took responsibility for causing the cosmetic damage, and was willing to cover the $2,212.30 bill to paint and replace the bumper cover, fog lights, and wheel liners. Then Crump asked for a full mechanical inspection, which revealed damaged tie rods and ball joints, jacking the bill beyond $6,000. Seibert's says it didn't cause this damage. Regardless of how it occurred, Seibert's insurer and Crump agree that her Hyundai is now a total loss due to the cost of the repairs it needs. It had been drivable, if mechanically worn, before police ordered it towed, damaging it for nothing more than a case of mistaken identity. The president of Seibert's towing told Moneywise that while they'd originally offered $2,200 to repair the bumper damage, Crump must now negotiate with their insurance company. Crump has now resorted to a GoFundMe campaign to attempt to raise $17,100 for rental car expenses, a new car, and the expenses of moving to a different neighborhood. 130 donors have already contributed $7,431.
Reached for comment, the Richmond Police Department told local newscasters they "understand that Ms. Crump did not ask to become part of this investigation," and that they recognize the "frustration of having a vehicle towed and subsequently damaged." But they also said they were following a "credible" lead, which is their responsibility. The department "appreciates Ms. Crump's cooperation" (and "sincerely hopes the remaining concerns about her vehicle can be resolved.")
The city of Richmond has "already started backing away from Flock before Crump's story aired," reports Moneywise. "Mayor Danny Avula has decided not to renew Richmond's license plate reader deal with Flock, which ends June 30, 2027. As of September, the city had 99 Flock readers on its streets."
They note that the Institute for Justice, a public interest law firm in Arlington, Virginia, "has tallied at least 27 cases since 2018" of similar police errors. "In each case, a license plate reader mistake led police to stop, jail or point guns at drivers who'd done nothing wrong. More than half came in 2023 or later."

item.title: Rocky Linux Creator Built a New 'Not Linux' Kernel in 11 Days Using AI
item.author: EditorDavid
item.content:encoded:
From the blog It's FOSS
Gregory Kurtzer is no stranger to the Linux world. He created CentOS, and when Red Hat messed it up, he started Rocky Linux as the community replacement. He also co-founded CIQ, the company offering enterprise support around Rocky. His latest project has nothing to do with rebuilding another Linux distro, though. He has built an entirely new operating system kernel, and he didn't write most of the code himself. An AI agent did. Meet Ginux, Linux userspace without Linux underneath... It's an independent, Rust-first x86-64 kernel. Which simply means it is NOT a fork of the Linux kernel. It has its own memory management, scheduler, process model, filesystems, networking, and device support, all written from scratch.
The most interesting part is that even though it is not Linux, it is Linux-compatible. Ginux implements the Linux ABI (the binary interface compiled programs use to talk to the kernel), so existing Linux binaries can run on it unmodified. In the project's own terms, Linux is a "personality" that Ginux exposes, not the kernel running underneath...
Right now, Ginux runs only in a QEMU virtual machine, with no physical hardware profile, no GPU or NVMe support, and no independent security audit.

item.title: Experts Expect 'Security Reckoning' As AI Tools Find And Exploit Software Bugs
item.author: EditorDavid
item.content:encoded:
The Washington Post reports:
Tens of thousands of South Koreans had their financial data exposed online in recent weeks after at least nine major banks there suffered cyberattacks that suggested a dark future for online security. One man, a 26-year-old living in southern China, was allegedly behind the attacks, according to an investigation by cybersecurity company CrowdStrike. Traces left online and failure to secure his own systems allowed investigators to piece together the man's name, age, location and what he allegedly did. The clues revealed that the devastating assault on some of Asia's most sophisticated financial institutions was the work of an amateur. The attacks were launched with help from a few artificial intelligence chatbots, CrowdStrike found, before asking one to help sell the stolen data online and draft a fake résumé touting cybersecurity skills...
The hacker who broke into the South Korean banks had access to Anthropic's Claude, but because the U.S. firm's tools generally refuse to take illegal actions, free Chinese models were also used, including DeepSeek, CrowdStrike found. "The models are interchangeable," said Meyers, the CrowdStrike executive.
The Post calls it "part of a wave of AI-enabled hacking that is advancing across the world, triggering alarm inside national governments as well as multinational companies."
"Basically any pedestrian, non-hacker can take these frameworks and start leveraging them to go after different targets," said Adam Meyers, senior vice president of counter adversary operations at CrowdStrike. The company has tracked an increase in the speed with which cyberattacks can move once inside a target's networks, as seasoned hackers and rank amateurs alike get a boost from AI tools. "Anyone can be a super-hacker now," Meyers said... Many cyber experts still expect the security reckoning to intensify as AI tools that can find and exploit software bugs become more widely distributed and understood.
[Last] Monday, The Post reported that cybersecurity researchers from the start-up Cathedral who set out to test Anthropic's security found that they could access internal messages and meeting transcripts. Cathedral reported its findings to Anthropic, which said it resolved the newly discovered problems... Security experts say it's unlikely that any hacker is forgoing the use of AI tools right now. Even in America, critical infrastructure like energy and water companies need to be "immediately and comprehensively" tested for exploitable bugs, according to Snehal Antani, chief executive of cybersecurity company Horizon3. He tells the Post the government might need to fund that remediation, and even form "a public and private partnership to accelerate incident response."

item.title: Stack Overflow: 'Reports of Our Death are Greatly Exaggerated'
item.author: EditorDavid
item.content:encoded:
Stack Overflow's senior VP of community says predictions of their demise "make for compelling headlines, but they confuse a change in how people access knowledge with the disappearance of the knowledge — and the company — behind it.
AI has changed developer behavior. In our recently released 2026 Developer Survey, 64% of respondents said they visit Stack Overflow less frequently for simple questions. But developers also report asking more advanced questions and visiting the site to verify AI-generated answers. Stack Overflow remains a place where people can challenge assumptions, compare approaches, and validate solutions.
But it's also important to understand that our public Q&A site is only one part of Stack Overflow, the company. The knowledge created on the Q&A site helps power the AI ecosystem itself. Stack Overflow's human-validated content is used to train and improve models, strengthen retrieval systems, and make AI assistants and other tools more reliable. Developers and technologists may encounter an answer through a different interface — such as their IDE — but the underlying knowledge may still have begun the same way it did in the past: with a developer sharing what they learned on Stack Overflow.
We're also building for what comes next. We recently launched the beta of Stack Overflow for Agents, an API-first knowledge exchange where agents can share knowledge and verify solutions. We also brought back Developer Story, giving developers a verifiable way to showcase their expertise, accomplishments, and contributions beyond a traditional résumé. And we have much more planned and in development to give people compelling new reasons to visit the site beyond Q&A.
Several years ago, we pivoted aggressively toward the enterprise. In September, we launched the next generation of Stack Internal, our governed AI context layer for companies. It captures and curates organizational knowledge, adds provenance and trust signals, and brings in subject-matter experts when validation is needed. The goal is straightforward: to make sure employees and AI agents are working from accurate, current, permission-aware information — not confidently acting on whatever context happens to be nearby.
That is the thread connecting everything we do: making human knowledge useful and trustworthy, whether it is being consumed by another developer, an enterprise team, or an AI agent. Stack Overflow is not standing still, and it is not disappearing. We are evolving from a website people visit for answers into knowledge infrastructure that supports developers, companies, and AI systems wherever they work. Reports of our death are, indeed, exaggerated.

item.title: SystemD's Creator Opens Signups for Private Preview of Amutable's Cryptographically Verified Linux Systems
item.author: EditorDavid
item.content:encoded:
SystemD creator Lennart Poettering left Red Hat for Microsoft in 2022, but 10 months ago left to co-found Amutable a company that aims to build cryptographically verified Linux systems that stay trusted over time.
It's FOSS calls it "a read-only, image-based system where every machine produces signed reports of its own state" — and signups are now open for a private preview:
Before announcing this Linux-based implementation, Amutable had released two open source tools. tine, a Buck2-based build system that composes OS images; available under MPL-2.0, and Quarry, a TUF-based tool that distributes those images to machines; available under Apache-2.0. What Amutable Foundations brings to the table is a service where Amutable runs the images, update repositories, control plane and vulnerability fixes for organizations and individuals who operate their own systems.
No license has been stated for those company-run parts, and the preview announcement does not say how much of Foundations beyond tine and Quarry will be open source. Software and configuration both ship as signed images, and a machine boots only what is signed. Because there is no package manager and no SSH or interactive shell, a change means giving every machine in your fleet a new signed image.
Its images are reproducible, come with a software bill of materials (SBOM) and are built from pinned inputs of whichever distribution you pick, with tine being able to import packages from Fedora or CentOS Stream. Each machine sends a signed report that records what it booted, from the firmware and boot loader up to the kernel and OS, plus the configuration it runs... Amutable's control plane verifies reports from systemd-report, an experimental command in systemd 260 that the company helped build. It compares each one with the declared state and flags machines that deviate. A rollout only continues while machines can show they are in a good state...
Amutable is signup formlooking for teams that manage Linux fleets and need to show what state each machine is in. It expects to start bringing the first 'design partners,' as it calls them, on board over the coming weeks.

item.title: Religious Exemption from Using AI in Workplace Granted to Humanist

"David Durman, a nontheistic humanist, recently secured a religious exemption from using AI in the workplace," reports TechCrunch.
Durman, a University of Kentucky administrator, told TechCrunch that humanism centers on "human well-being and flourishing, both individually and collectively ... and implores a person to try to improve both their well-being and their flourishing as well as the others around them." He believes that using the technology runs counter to his beliefs. "The way we become moral actors for ourselves and for others is through the active application of our minds, and the diminishing of that [through AI use] is going to necessarily have a negative impact on our ability to do so," he said, reflecting on how overreliance on AI might affect critical thinking...."
[Humanism] tends to appeal to people who are skeptical of a god or other supernatural power yet still seek a scientific and moral framework to ground themselves in. [Alexandria Huiskens, staff attorney at the American Humanist Association, told TechCrunch] "Concern about AI and human dignity can run through several different faiths and traditions, whether that's Catholic teachings, or Universalism, or Humanism, and we want Humanists or nontheists to know that they fall into these categories — that they are also protected by the law at work...."
In Durman's administrative role, in which he supports researchers applying for grants, he has not been required to use AI at work. Like many workers across fields, some of his colleagues and leadership have recommended that employees try out these tools, so he sought to secure his exemption now, in case the suggestion becomes a mandate in the future. "I hope that if [others] have similar feelings, that they feel encouraged to pursue some kind of resolution," Durman said.
A University of Kentucky spokesperson told TechCrunch they "determined that an accommodation could be provided while allowing the employee to continue performing the essential functions of their position." Speaking on Tesla's call about his work on humanoid robots, Musk said, "Some of them look very impressive, but they're not really using any kind of advanced AI or SI." Zuckerberg was equally compliant on Meta's earnings call on Oct. 21, emphasizing his company's "goal of delivering personal superintelligence to everyone." However, Meta was already using the term, having created a unit called Meta Superintelligence Labs last year....
[Some other tech CEOs are holding out.] Amazon CEO Andy Jassy peppered his call with use of "AI" on Thursday, uttering the abbreviation well over a dozen times in his introductory remarks. A day earlier, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said one of the company's three points of focus is "designing AI to empower people." Trump's preferred term is seeping into other correspondence and documents. Microsoft's annual report, filed last week, included eight mentions of "super intelligence," starting at the top of the letter to shareholders... IBM CEO Arvind Krishna, who didn't attend Trump's September lunch, used "SI" alongside "AI" during his company's earnings call last week.... Lip-Bu Tan, CEO of chipmaker Intel, said Thursday the supply shortage the chip industry is navigating has been "driven by the unprecedented demand for super intelligence."
Some in the tech industry have been explicit in their support of Trump's terminology ahead of their forthcoming earnings reports next month. Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora repeatedly referred to "SI" on CNBC, and posted on X on Sept. 30, "The meeting at the WH on SI was an epic moment...." But the article also includes a quote from media/technology studies professor Torin Monahan at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. item.title: America's Clocks Are Still Falling Back Tonight Despite Trump's Daylight Saving Push
item.author: EditorDavid
item.content:encoded:
Clocks "fall back" one hour tonight to end Daylight Saving Time — though many Americans want to end the twice-yearly clock change, reports Axios.
But the U.S. Congress "remains deadlocked about how to make that happen."
The clocks are falling back despite a bipartisan House vote in July to make daylight saving time permanent and Trump's subsequent push for Senate action... While most Americans want to end the twice-yearly clock changes, they don't necessarily favor Trump's solution. Gallup found 48% of Americans support permanent standard time the entire year, compared with 24% who prefer permanent daylight saving time, as Trump wants... In 1974, the U.S. experimented with year-round daylight saving time but reversed course amid concerns about children going to school in the dark>.
Experts still debate whether permanent DST is good for people. Supporters argue that permanent daylight saving time would provide more afternoon and evening sunlight, encouraging outdoor activities. But sleep experts warn that darker mornings and lighter evenings can disrupt sleep cycles, while permanent daylight saving time could force millions of children to travel to school in the dark. The bottom line: The American Academy of Sleep Medicine says it prefers permanent standard time because it better aligns with natural sleep cycles.
"Hawaii and most of Arizona don't observe daylight saving time, so their clocks won't change," the article points out, adding that eliminating it for the rest of America "still faces opposition in the Senate and isn't expected to be considered by the end of the year.
But "the upcoming midterms could change the balance of power in Congress, potentially shifting the debate."

item.title: Xbox Manager: AI Already Being Used In Xbox Game Development - And Throughout the Game Industry
item.author: EditorDavid
item.content:encoded:
Should generative AI be used for videogame development? Brandon Stirrup, a strategy manager at Xbox, claims Xbox is already using AI, reports Engadget. And he also says that those who say they aren't are merely "pretending."
Stirrup deactivated his social media account shortly after (though his posts have been archived elsewhere), igniting conversations about what role generative AI actually has or should have in game development. In some ways, it would be unsurprising to learn that Xbox is using AI to the extent that Stirrup implies. Xbox recently announced the formation of Xbox Labs at least in part as a response to a rising trend of AI-coded game ports; the announcement heavily implied that the new team would use AI as well but didn't say it outright. Xbox owner Microsoft is also a major player in AI development... Developers including Capcom, Square Enix, Sega, Nexon and Activision have all either used AI in their games or pledged to do so. Fortnite developer Epic Games has been particularly up-front about its AI use, and CEO Tim Sweeney has aggressively promoted it on social media...
On the other hand, there are large pockets of the game industry vocally opposed to generative AI. Notably, these tend to be smaller, independent studios without shareholders to impress by touting the cost-savings of AI. These studios include Tunic publisher Finji, Stardew Valley developer ConcernedApe and Clickolding developer Strange Scaffold, among many more. Due to the sheer number and variety of game studios, it's impossible to say just how much of the industry actually uses AI at this point, but claims that "everyone" is using it are clearly false.
There's a similar divide among players about whether generative AI should be embraced or avoided at all costs. While some simply accept AI as part of games going forward, others have pledged to avoid games that use the technology outright due to its environmental costs, labor issues or pure aesthetic preference. That's led to the popularity of tools like a browser extension that makes Steam's AI disclosures more visible and grassroots efforts by developers to implement labels certifying their games as AI-free... Many players and developers alike justify the use of AI in generating code, even if they're opposed to it in other areas.
"Gaming is the only industry slow-walking the transition," Xbox's Stirrup allegedly said, "because users have negative sentiment. Everyone else accepts reality."
"Gaming is the only industry pretending to not use AI."
